title: Buy Risk, Sell Certainty: Where the Money Lives in Off-Plan Real Estate
seoTitle: Where the Money Lives in Off-Plan Real Estate
description: Off-plan prices follow certainty, not the unit. How deposits, assignments and the developer's incentives create profit, with a worked example and five rules.
answer: An off-plan unit's price tracks how certain buyers are that it will exist, not the unit itself. You buy the right to purchase at a fixed price while risk is high, then assign that right to a later buyer who pays more for certainty. The gap, minus fees and taxes, is your profit.
body:
Buying off-plan is one of the riskiest moves in real estate and one of the most profitable. Both are true for the same reason.

## Price follows certainty

When you commit off-plan, the building exists only as a plan. Where your unit will be, there may be a parking lot. Nobody pays full price for a parking lot, so you pay the lowest price that unit will ever have.

Two years later, the same unit has the same layout, the same view and the same finishes. Yet it costs more. Nothing changed inside it. What changed is how sure people are that it will exist. **Off-plan prices are not really about the unit. They are about the risk attached to it.**

## What you actually buy

You sign a contract and pay a deposit, usually a small share of the price, often in stages as construction advances. You do not own a property. You own the **right to buy** a property at a fixed price on a future date. That right is the asset, and like any asset it can be worth more later than you paid for it.

## Why the developer wants what you want

The obvious fear is that the developer will not deliver. Look at it from their side. Their profit on the project is many times yours, roughly ten times in my experience. Their reputation is on the line, and they need this project finished to launch the next one, where their future income is. You and the developer want exactly the same outcome: a building finished on time, on budget, and looking like the promise.

## Moving from one side to the other

At the start, risk is high and price is low. At the end, risk is low and price is high. You earn by moving between the two, and you do not have to wait for the keys. You **assign** the contract: you sell your right to buy to someone else before completion.

**A worked example.** You commit to a $500,000 unit at presale with a $50,000 deposit. Two years later the structure is up and similar units sell for $600,000. A new buyer takes over your contract, returns your $50,000 and pays you the $100,000 difference. You put $50,000 to work and made $100,000 before fees and taxes, without ever owning the property. The new buyer is not losing either: they paid more for much less risk.

## Assignments are not automatic

Your contract decides whether, when and at what cost you can assign. In many markets the developer must approve it, which is normal: they need to know the next buyer can close. In British Columbia, assignments are also reported to a provincial register. Taxes matter too. In Canada, assignment sales of new homes and condos have been subject to GST/HST since May 2022, and profits must be declared. Some developers charge an assignment fee. None of this breaks the model. It simply means your real profit is the gap minus the total cost.

## What creates certainty

Cranes on site, floors going up, new buyers arriving. Each time buyers can see more of what they are getting, risk drops a little and price climbs a little. For years the only way to see was to wait for concrete. Today a developer can show every buyer their exact unit before it exists: the space, the real view from that floor, its place in the project. The developer sells faster, the first buyer knows what they are committing to, and the next buyer knows what they are paying for.

## Five rules before you commit

1. **Plan the exit before the entry.** Decide roughly when you would assign and at what price. If you cannot picture the next buyer, think twice.
2. **Check the developer's finished work.** Past buildings tell you more than any brochure.
3. **Compare presale prices with finished buildings nearby.** If they already match, there is no gap left to capture.
4. **Make sure you can carry every deposit.** Plan as if you will pay all of them, not assign before they are due.
5. **Read the assignment clause with a lawyer.** Consent, fees, timing and marketing limits decide your exit.

You buy the risk. You sell certainty. That is where the money lives.
takeaways: Off-plan prices track certainty, not the unit itself.
A presale contract is a right to buy at a fixed price, and that right can rise in value.
Developers are strongly motivated to deliver because their profit dwarfs yours.
Your real profit is the price gap minus assignment fees, taxes and costs.
Plan your exit, check the developer's past and make sure you can carry every deposit.
faq: Selling your contract, the right to buy a unit at a fixed price, to a new buyer before the building is finished. The new buyer takes your place with the developer.
Are off-plan assignments taxed in Canada?
Yes. Since May 2022 assignment sales of new homes and condos are subject to GST/HST, and profits must be reported on your tax return.
Does the developer have to approve an assignment?
In many contracts, yes. Developers want to confirm the new buyer can close, and some charge a fee or restrict timing.
How do I know if there is still profit in a presale?
Compare the presale price per square foot with finished buildings nearby. If they are already equal, the gap that pays early buyers is gone.
